item.title: As these network attacks and impersonation attempts happen, who's securing the elderly? Especially thinking about my parents and grandparents. There are four layers I can think through where this could work. One is at the browser level, where somebody builds a secure browser that ensures that wh...
item.description:
作者：Nikunj Kothari 账号：@nikunj 简介：partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early hire @meter, @opendoor, @atlassian & others. love @shimoleejhaveri + 👦👧
As these network attacks and impersonation attempts happen, who's securing the elderly?
Especially thinking about my parents and grandparents.
There are four layers I can think through where this could work.
One is at the browser level, where somebody builds a secure browser that ensures that whatever websites they're going to are secured. Texts typically lead to a link, even for payments. This is why browser is key.
Two could be at the network layer, where there is a physical device, similar to Pi-hole, or an Onavo-like VPN on your phone, that blocks websites that could be deemed unsafe.
Three could be at the payments layer, where transactions that look like scams get flagged before the money leaves.
And fourth and most crazy could be at the phone level, where everything is monitored, and you're only getting calls from your loved ones. Cloned voices would work with a provider like Reality Defender.
There are individual solutions for this today but none neatly packaged.
This could all be packaged with insurance that covers any activities on the OS or phone. In that way, incentives are aligned to keep this on the edge.
The buyer would be the kids, someone like me, who get alerted when something looks off.

item.title: Superintelligence Needs the Physical World with CEO and Co-Founder of Arda Bob McGrew
item.description:
播客：No Priors
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:17 If you look around outside, how different is anything from ten years ago before AI happened? Not very different at all. The first time you were in your Waymo, you thought to yourself, this is amazing. Probably the third time you're in your Waymo, you're like, man, this traffic sucks. We need to break out of this pure focus on the digital world and go to the physical world.
Speaker 1 | 00:17 - 00:22 I don't think you are actually gonna be able to get to superintelligence without changes in the physical world.
Speaker 2 | 00:28 - 00:54 Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, Elad and I are here with Bob McGrew, the CEO and cofounder of Arda. Bob was previously an early key exec at Palantir and the chief research officer at OpenAI. We talk about making American manufacturing competitive with intelligence, why physical intelligence is necessary for superintelligence, and why the future is going to be machines that can make machines and explore the stars.
Speaker 2 | 00:54 - 00:55 Welcome, Bob.
Speaker 3 | 00:55 - 00:59 Bob, thanks so much for joining us today. No priors. Great to be here. Yeah. So you've had a ridiculous career.
Speaker 3 | 00:59 - 01:31 You were the chief research officer at OpenAI, so you drove all those sort of research directions for the company or at least set a lot of the agenda. You were at Palantir quite early and one of the main people there driving product and engineering. So you've had this amazing career spanning some of the most seminal moments of the digital world, and yet now you're working in the physical world. And it's right in the arrow when people are talking about RSI, which is recursive self improvement, about how we will no longer have researchers and be displaced displaced by code and AI and, you know, AI building itself. Why do anything in the physical world right now as this digital revolution is happening?
Speaker 1 | 01:31 - 01:59 Well, you know, fundamentally, I don't think you are actually gonna be able to get to superintelligence without changes in the physical world. So, you know, the... We've seen a huge amount of improvement from ChatGPT, from agents. You know, all of this is happening in our digital lives, and very little of that has actually affected the atoms of our lives. Like, if you look around outside, how different is anything from ten years ago before AI happened?
Speaker 1 | 01:59 - 01:59 Mhmm.
Speaker 3 | 01:59 - 01:59 You know?
Speaker 1 | 01:59 - 02:05 Not very different at all. You know? Even when you're doing something that is genuinely very different. Maybe you're in a self driving car. Right?
Speaker 1 | 02:05 - 02:20 You're, you know, in a self driving car, in your Waymo, going around San Francisco. And the first time you were in your Waymo, you thought to yourself, this is amazing. There's there's no one driving it. The, like, car is driving itself. And, like, probably the third time you're in your Waymo, you're like, traffic.
Speaker 1 | 02:20 - 02:29 Man, this traffic sucks. Yeah. Right? Because just, you know, you have something... Even, you know, a Waymo is, like, halfway towards the physical world, but, like, you didn't change the car.
Speaker 1 | 02:29 - 02:50 Like, the car doesn't fly. You're still bounded by all of the physical barriers that, you know, made the car trips around San Francisco pretty, slow even in the nineteen nineties. Right? And so fundamentally, we need to break out of this pure focus on the digital world and go to the physical world.
Speaker 3 | 02:50 - 02:55 So when you say you can't have superintelligence without changing the physical world, what does that actually mean? Yes. What does that substantiate us?
Speaker 1 | 02:55 - 03:15 So so maybe a good place to start here is I think there's this common perception and... Or there's a common argument, and I've I've been hearing it since, like, 2018, which says that if you can just automate the work of the researcher, that you're gonna be able to unleash a runaway acceleration, runaway self improvement loop, and we're gonna have a singularity.
Speaker 2 | 03:15 - 03:16 This is the hard takeoff.
Speaker 1 | 03:16 - 03:21 Yeah. Hard takeoff. Exactly. And I think this is wrong. I think this this argument is just straightforwardly wrong.
Speaker 1 | 03:21 - 03:33 So, you know, just to recapitulate the argument, it says, you know, okay. So we can automate 10% of a research time. That is gonna give... You know, that's gonna give some improvement. We automate 50% of a researcher's time.
Speaker 1 | 03:33 - 03:54 Now you have a two x improvement. So now you're going two x faster. And then you automate 90% of a researcher's time, you're going 10 x faster. 99% automated, you're going a 100 x faster. And so by automating more and more of this job, you know, and eliminating this labor of the researcher, you're able to just, you know, zoom up and have runaway acceleration.
Speaker 1 | 03:54 - 04:09 But this is this is this is straightforwardly wrong because researchers are not the bottleneck. Right? Like, the amount of time it takes in order for you to discover something is not primarily bounded by the number of researchers you have. Fundamentally, those researchers are running experiments.
Speaker 3 | 04:09 - 04:10 Mhmm.
Speaker 1 | 04:10 - 04:29 And so, you know, if you if you actually think about the the... You know, even today, right, even two years ago in 2024 when I was chief research officer at OpenAI, like, the actual limiting factor was not the number of researchers we could hire. It was the amount of GPUs that we had on hand. Mhmm. It was the physical amount of compute that we were able to put out there.
Speaker 1 | 04:29 - 04:41 And, you know, was the compute accumulated in the right places? Was it connected together with the right networks? And so you can, you know, completely automate researchers. This is a big effect. Right?
Speaker 1 | 04:41 - 05:09 I'm not saying this is not a big deal. You know, maybe this is even... Maybe the ability to do automated research is gonna be as impactful as the ability to go from, you know, GPD four o without reasoning to o three with reasoning and tools. That was a huge one time acceleration, but it's not RSI. So I think the right way to think about research is that, you know, fundamentally, there's a bunch of experiments.
Speaker 1 | 05:09 - 05:17 You have to run these experiments. And right now there's a lot of waste. You have to... You know, researchers have to do a lot of engineering. They have to pick the right experiments.
Speaker 1 | 05:18 - 05:45 They have to just, you know, go physically schedule them on the GPUs, and all of these lead to the GPUs being less effective at delivering new discoveries. And so, you know, the correct mental model is to look at the GPUs and to say, okay. Well, you know, right now, the GPUs are 35% of the way to optimal in order to be able to deliver discoveries. And if we can automate more and more, maybe we can get them to 90% of the way to optimal. Mhmm.
Speaker 1 | 05:45 - 06:09 But the difference between going from 90 to 99% of optimal, it's actually not a big difference. And so we can automate researchers. It's a big one time benefit, but it doesn't kick in a self improvement cycle. Instead, it's one more, you know, s curve, one more big one time improvement similar to reasoning that allows us to, you know, get closer to optimum. Mhmm.
Speaker 1 | 06:09 - 06:10 And then we have to go do something else.
Speaker 3 | 06:10 - 06:29 Yeah. I feel like a lot of AI driven research is basically stacking S curves of different types, or AI development, should say, in That also translates into other domains, though. There's robotics, there's biology, there's a few other places where the physical world is really, you know, the primary limiter on progress. Right? You have to run the biology experiment.
Speaker 3 | 06:29 - 07:00 You have to build the, you know, the motors for the the so...
